#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Compensation Survey (NCS)
Description: The National Compensation Survey (NCS) is conducted by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics to collect data on wages and benefits for America's workforce. Data gathered through the NCS is used to generate the Employment Cost Index (ECI), Employer Costs for Employee Compensation (ECEC), Employee Benefits, and Modeled Wage Estimates (MWE).

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Handbook of Methods Employment Cost Index Overview

Employment Cost Index: Overview

The Employment Cost Index (ECI) measures the change in the hourly labor cost to employers over time. The ECI uses a fixed “basket” of labor to produce a pure cost change, free from the effects of workers moving between occupations and industries, and includes both the cost of wages and salaries and the cost of benefits. These data are collected through the National Compensation Survey (NCS) and provide information about compensation costs over time.

Quick Facts: Employment Cost Index
Subject areas Benefits, Pay
Key measures
  • Indexes
  • 3-month and 12-month percent changes
  • Seasonally adjusted and not seasonally adjusted
  • Current and constant dollar

Handbook of Methods Employer Costs for Employee Compensation Overview

Employer Costs for Employee Compensation: Overview

The Employer Costs for Employee Compensation (ECEC) measures the average employer’s cost per employee hour worked for total compensation, wages and salaries, benefits, and costs as a percentage of total compensation. Employer costs are available for different benefits, including paid leave vacation, holiday, sick, and personal leave; supplemental pay, including overtime and premium, shift differentials, and nonproduction bonuses; insurance, including life, health, and short-term and long-term disability; retirement and savings, including defined benefit and defined contribution; and legally required benefits, including Social Security, Medicare, federal and state unemployment insurance, and workers’ compensation. These data are collected through the National Compensation Survey (NCS) and provide information about average compensation in the economy at a point in time.

Quick Facts: Employer Costs for Employee Compensation
Subject areas Pay, Benefits
Key measures
  • Cost per hour worked
  • Percent of total compensation
  • Compensation percentiles
How the data are obtained Survey of businesses, Government agencies

Handbook of Methods Employer Costs for Employee Compensation Calculation

Employer Costs for Employee Compensation: Calculation

The Employer Costs for Employee Compensation (ECEC) is a product of the National Compensation Survey (NCS) that collects data on employer costs for employer-provided wages and salaries and benefits. The calculation details for the ECEC are covered in this section.

Measuring costs

The ECEC measures the average costs to employers for wages and salaries and benefits per employee hour worked.

Exhibit 1. Benefit costs measured by the ECEC

Cost data are presented both in dollar amounts and as percentages of total compensation. Cost data are published quarterly.

The ECEC series provides an average cost across all workers. Eligible workers with access to employer-sponsored benefits who do not participate are also included in the calculation. That is, the average cost includes both workers for whom the employer incurred a compensation cost and those for whom no cost was incurred.

To calculate cost levels, the ECEC uses current employment weights to reflect the changing composition of today’s labor force. The employment weights are derived from two BLS programs: the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) and the Current Employment Statistics (CES). Combined, these programs provide the appropriate industry coverage and the right timeframe of the data needed to benchmark (post-stratify) employment weights for the ECEC series.

In most instances, private industry employment weights used in the ECEC are total employment estimates for two-digit industry groups, such as utilities (NAICS 22) or wholesale trade (NAICS 42). In a few cases, the employment weights associated with more detailed industrial categories are used. This includes the four-digit NAICS categories elementary and secondary schools (6111), junior colleges (6122), colleges and universities (6133); and the six-digit NAICS category aircraft manufacturing (336411). For state and local governments, the ECEC uses a more aggregated level, reflecting the level of detail published by the Current Employment Statistics (CES) program.

DEPARTMENT OF LABOR

Bureau of Labor Statistics


Information Collection Activities; Comment Request

AGENCY: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Department of Labor.

ACTION: Notice of information collection; request for comment.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Department of Labor, as part of its continuing effort to 
reduce paperwork and respondent burden, conducts a pre-clearance 
consultation program to provide the general public and Federal agencies 
with an opportunity to comment on proposed and/or continuing 
collections of information in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction 
Act of 1995. This program helps to ensure that requested data can be 
provided in the desired format, reporting burden (time and financial 
resources) is minimized, collection instruments are clearly understood, 
and the impact of collection requirements on respondents can be 
properly assessed. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) is soliciting 
comments concerning the proposed revision of the ``National 
Compensation Survey.'' A copy of the proposed information collection 
request can be obtained by contacting the individual listed below in 
the Addresses section of this notice.

DATES: Written comments must be submitted to the office listed in the 
Addresses section of this notice on or before September 15, 2025.

ADDRESSES: Send comments to Nora Kincaid, BLS Clearance Officer, 
Division of Management Systems, Bureau of Labor Statistics, by email to 
[email protected].

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Nora Kincaid, BLS Clearance Officer, 
at 202-691-7628 (this is not a toll free number.) (See Addresses 
section.)

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Background

    The National Compensation Survey (NCS) is a nation-wide survey of 
private industry establishments and state and local governments that 
provides comprehensive measures of (1) employer costs for employee

[[Page 32030]]

compensation, including wages and salaries, and benefits, (2) 
compensation trends, and (3) the incidence of employer-sponsored 
benefits among workers. The NCS also collects data and produces 
estimates on the provisions of selected employer-sponsored benefit 
plans. The NCS produces:
     Indexes measuring change over time in labor costs through 
the Employment Cost Index (ECI), a Principal Federal Economic Indicator 
(PFEI).
     The level of average costs per hour worked through the 
Employer Costs for Employee Compensation (ECEC).
     Estimates on the incidence of benefits by the percentage 
of workers with access to and participating in employer-sponsored 
benefit plans, as well as details of what those plans provide, in the 
publication of the Employee Benefits in the United States.
     Details of employer-provided health and retirement plan 
provisions in the Health and Retirement Plan Provision publications.
     Occupational wage data by work level for use by the 
President's Pay Agent, meeting the requirements of the Federal 
Employees Pay Comparability Act of 1990 (FEPCA). This data is produced 
in collaboration with the BLS' Occupational Employment and Wage 
Statistics (OEWS) program.

II. Current Action

    Office of Management and Budget clearance is being sought for a 
revision of the NCS.
    The NCS is designed to be a national representative survey of 
private industry and state and local government establishments from all 
50 states and the District of Columbia. The NCS private industry sample 
is on a three-year rotational cycle, with one frozen sample year 
approximately every ten years for the NCS private industry sample when 
a new NCS State and local government sample is under collection.
    The NCS collects occupational information and wage and benefit data 
from a sample of employers. Using probability sampling, the NCS selects 
up to eight jobs at an establishment and collects job information, 
including job duties and work level characteristics, and wages and 
benefit information. Benefit information includes the incidence, costs, 
and provisions of the employer-provided benefits. The BLS updates the 
wage and benefit cost data quarterly. Updating this information allows 
for the publication of change in the cost of wages, benefits, and total 
compensation on a quarterly basis as a measure of labor market 
inflation.
    The NCS employs various methods to collect data from 
establishments. NCS policy is to collect the data in whichever form is 
easiest for the respondents to provide. Respondents may choose to send 
the data on forms that the BLS provides. The respondents may respond 
through email, fax, mail, telephone, or a secure BLS website.
    The BLS is planning to eliminate several NCS data elements to 
reduce the annual costs and burden of the survey. The data elements are 
not considered to be heavily used or in public demand based on metrics 
from public database hits and customer service inquiries. The 
collection and review of these elements are resource intensive. The 
elements planned for removal capture:
     The presence of and plan details for sick leave carry 
over.
     The presence of retiree life.
     The presence of third-party plan administration and stop 
loss protection for health insurance.
     Employee non-medical premiums.
     Employer non-medical premiums when expenditures are 
collected or costs are unknown.
     Plan details for Defined Benefit Frozen Plans.
     The presence of Other Benefits plans or provisions of 
plans.
    The BLS is planning to discontinue the collection of Worker's 
Compensation Insurance due to the BLS's inability to improve the 
currently low response rate for this benefit. Further response efforts 
could potentially lead to lower response rates for other benefits, 
which make up a larger proportion of total compensation.
    The BLS is also planning a re-weight of the ECI to update 
employment counts as was done multiple times in the past.

III. Desired Focus of Comments

    The Bureau of Labor Statistics is particularly interested in 
comments that:
     Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is 
necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, 
including whether the information will have practical utility.
     Evaluate the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the 
burden of the proposed collection of information, including the 
validity of the methodology and assumptions used.
     Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the 
information to be collected.
     Minimize the burden of the collection of information on 
those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate 
automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection 
techniques or other forms of information technology, e.g., permitting 
electronic submissions of responses.

                                  EMPLOYMENT COST INDEX � SEPTEMBER 2024

Compensation costs for civilian workers increased 0.8 percent, seasonally adjusted, for the 3-month period 
ending in September 2024, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Wages and salaries increased 
0.8 percent and benefit costs increased 0.8 percent from June 2024. (See tables A, 1, 2, and 3.)

Compensation costs for civilian workers increased 3.9 percent for the 12-month period ending in September 
2024 and increased 4.3 percent in September 2023. Wages and salaries increased 3.9 percent for the 12-month
period ending in September 2024 and increased 4.6 percent for the 12-month period ending in September 2023.
Benefit costs increased 3.7 percent over the year and increased 4.1 percent for the 12-month period ending 
in September 2023. (See tables A, 4, 8, and 12.)

Compensation costs for private industry workers increased 3.6 percent over the year. In September 2023, the
increase was 4.3 percent. Wages and salaries increased 3.8 percent for the 12-month period ending in 
September 2024 and increased 4.5 percent in September 2023. The cost of benefits increased 3.3 percent for
the 12-month period ending in September 2024 and increased 3.9 percent in September 2023. 
Inflation-adjusted (constant dollar) wages and salaries increased 1.2 percent for the 12 months ending 
September 2024. (See tables A, 5, 9, and 12.) 

Within private industry by bargaining status, compensation costs increased 5.8 percent for union workers 
and 3.4 percent for non-union workers for the 12-month period ending in September 2024. Wages and salaries 
increased 6.4 percent for union workers and 3.6 percent for non-union workers for the 12-month period 
ending in September 2024. Benefit costs increased 4.9 percent for union workers and 3.1 percent for 
non-union workers for the period ending in September 2024. (See tables 6, 10, and 12.)

Compensation costs for state and local government workers increased 4.7 percent for the 12-month period 
ending in September 2024 and increased 4.8 percent in September 2023. Wages and salaries increased 4.6 
percent for the 12-month period ending in September 2024 and 4.8 percent from a year ago. Benefit costs 
increased 4.8 percent for the 12-month period ending in September 2024. The prior year�s increase was 4.7 
percent. (See tables A, 7, 11, and 12.)

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Compensation Survey (NCS)
Description: The National Compensation Survey (NCS) is conducted by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics to collect data on wages and benefits for America's workforce. Data gathered through the NCS is used to generate the Employment Cost Index (ECI), Employer Costs for Employee Compensation (ECEC), Employee Benefits, and Modeled Wage Estimates (MWE).

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# National Compensation Survey (NCS): research and preservation report

**Research checked:** October 9, 2026  
**Primary sources:** U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Office of Management and Budget (OMB), and Federal Register documentation.

## Executive findings

Your description is **substantially accurate**, with two important qualifications:

1. **NCS is a survey program and a family of statistical products—not one downloadable dataset.** Its underlying establishment and job records are confidential; its public outputs are estimates, time series, tables, and publications.
2. **Modeled Wage Estimates (MWE) combine NCS data with Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) data.** They are not generated from NCS alone.

A more precise catalog description would be:

> The National Compensation Survey is a voluntary, establishment-based survey conducted by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, U.S. Department of Labor. It collects information on wages and salaries, employer benefit costs, benefit access and participation, benefit-plan provisions, and job characteristics for workers in private industry and state and local government. NCS supplies the data for the Employment Cost Index, Employer Costs for Employee Compensation, and Employee Benefits statistics, and contributes to Modeled Wage Estimates produced jointly from NCS and Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics data. Federal employees, agricultural workers, private-household workers, and the self-employed are outside its principal coverage.

**Preservation priority: high.** NCS supports monetary policy, federal and military pay decisions, Medicare payment adjustments, collective bargaining, and analysis of employer-sponsored benefits. Its long history, changing classifications, revised time series, confidential microdata, and dispersed publication formats make preservation of **documentation and release vintages** as important as preservation of numerical values.

Sources: [NCS overview](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ncs/home.htm), [current ECI data-source documentation](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/eci/data.htm), [MWE concepts](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/mwe/concepts.htm).

---

## 1. Identity, publisher, and institutional responsibility

| Attribute | Finding |
|---|---|
| Official program name | National Compensation Survey |
| Acronym | NCS |
| Publisher and statistical producer | U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics |
| Parent department | U.S. Department of Labor |
| Data source | Employers: private establishments and state/local government establishments |
| Survey character | Voluntary probability sample; ongoing collection with rotating samples |
| Principal subject areas | Pay, employer compensation costs, employee benefits, job characteristics |
| Public data level | Statistical estimates for groups—not identifiable employer or employee records |
| OMB control number | **1220-0164** |
| Major outputs | ECI, ECEC, Employee Benefits; input to MWE |
| Geographic scope | Establishments in the 50 states and District of Columbia; published detail varies by product |

BLS designs the survey, collects and reviews responses, calculates estimates, screens outputs for confidentiality and reliability, and publishes results.

The name **Employee Benefits Survey (EBS)** persists in BLS web addresses and historical documentation. Current methods documentation calls the output program **Employee Benefits**, whose data are collected through NCS.

An important documentation change: BLS has divided the former unified NCS *Handbook of Methods* chapter into separate chapters for **ECI, ECEC, and Employee Benefits**. The old NCS chapter remains an archive, not the best sole source for current methodology.

Sources: [archived NCS methods overview](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ncs/home.htm), [Employee Benefits overview](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/eb/home.htm), [OMB collection record](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202506-1220-001).

## 2. Authority, mandates, and legal governance

### General statistical authority

BLS identifies **29 U.S.C. § 2b** as authority to conduct continuing studies of labor costs across manufacturing, mining, transportation, distribution, and other industries.

### Federal pay mandates

The **Federal Employees Pay Comparability Act of 1990 (FEPCA)** establishes important uses of BLS compensation statistics:

- **5 U.S.C. § 5303:** annual adjustments to federal pay schedules.
- **5 U.S.C. § 5304:** locality-based comparability payments and surveys comparing federal and nonfederal pay.

These are distinct functions. The **ECI** informs the general pay-adjustment formula; BLS wage and work-level information contributes to locality comparisons used by the **President’s Pay Agent**.

The current OMB inventory also lists **5 U.S.C. § 5318** and **2 U.S.C. § 4501**, concerning adjustments to certain federal pay rates and congressional compensation. These are downstream statutory uses, not a requirement that every sampled employer participate.

### Military pay

BLS documents statutory linkage of military basic-pay adjustments to the ECI under **37 U.S.C. § 1009**, as amended by the FY2004 National Defense Authorization Act. Actual annual pay decisions can be affected by subsequent legislation or authorized alternatives; an index linkage should not be interpreted as an unconditional prediction of the eventual increase.

### Paperwork Reduction Act approval

Collection is reviewed under the **Paperwork Reduction Act**, with public-comment notices and OMB approval.

The latest collection record located in this research:

- **ICR:** 202506-1220-001
- **OMB control number:** 1220-0164
- **Approval:** May 6, 2026
- **Expiration:** May 31, 2029
- **Status:** Active

**Key distinction:** BLS has authority and statutory responsibilities to produce compensation statistics, but **NCS participation is voluntary**.

### Economic-indicator governance

The ECI is designated a **Principal Federal Economic Indicator** under OMB Statistical Policy Directive No. 3. That status matters for scheduled dissemination and management of market-sensitive statistics.

Sources: [current OMB record](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202506-1220-001), [2018 supporting statement explaining statutory authority](https://omb.report/icr/201712-1220-003/doc/81468201.pdf), [BLS documented uses](https://www.bls.gov/eci/overview/national-compensation-survey-usage.htm).

## 3. What the public products measure

| Product | Main question answered | Measures and frequency | Important distinction |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Employment Cost Index (ECI)** | How quickly are employers’ labor costs changing? | Quarterly indexes and 3- and 12-month changes; wages, benefits, total compensation; selected seasonally adjusted and constant-dollar series | Holds industry/occupation employment composition fixed to reduce composition effects |
| **Employer Costs for Employee Compensation (ECEC)** | What does compensation cost employers at a point in time? | Quarterly dollars per employee hour worked and percentages of total compensation | Uses current employment weights; changes can reflect both costs and workforce composition |
| **Employee Benefits** | Who has employer-sponsored benefits, and what do those plans provide? | Annual access, participation, take-up, premium-sharing and selected plan-provision statistics | Benefits offered, benefits available to workers, and participation are different measures |
| **Modeled Wage Estimates (MWE)** | What are occupational hourly wages by job characteristics and location? | Annual modeled mean hourly wages, with relative standard errors | Combines NCS job-characteristic information with OEWS occupational/geographic detail |

### Compensation components

ECEC documentation identifies:

- **Paid leave:** vacation, holidays, sick and personal leave.
- **Supplemental pay:** overtime/premium pay, shift differentials, nonproduction bonuses.
- **Insurance:** health, life, short- and long-term disability.
- **Retirement and savings:** defined-benefit and defined-contribution plans.
- **Legally required benefits:** Social Security, Medicare, unemployment insurance, and historically workers’ compensation.

**The component list is changing:** see Section 10 for announced workers’ compensation changes.

### Benefits concepts that must remain distinct

- **Access:** a benefit plan is available for the employee’s use.
- **Participation:** the employee is counted as participating under the applicable plan rules.
- **Take-up rate:** participants divided by workers with access, multiplied by 100.
- **Establishment offering a benefit:** at least some workers in the establishment have access.

Take-up rates calculated from published rounded access and participation percentages may not reproduce the official rate exactly.

Sources: [ECI overview](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/eci/home.htm), [ECEC overview](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ecec/home.htm), [benefits concepts](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/eb/concepts.htm), [MWE calculation](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/mwe/calculation.htm).

## 4. Population, geography, and analytical dimensions

### Covered population

The principal NCS population consists of employees in:

- Private industry, including covered nonprofit establishments.
- State and local government.

In NCS publications, **“civilian workers” means the combination of those two groups**. It does **not** mean every civilian worker in the United States.

### Major exclusions

BLS identifies exclusions including:

- Federal government and quasi-federal agencies.
- Military personnel.
- Agriculture.
- Private households.
- Self-employed workers and workers who set their own pay.
- Certain unpaid, volunteer, overseas, and other out-of-scope workers.

Thus, federal and military pay can be **affected by** NCS statistics even though those employees are not the survey’s principal measured population.

### Published breakdowns

Depending on product and period, estimates distinguish:

- Industry and occupational groups.
- Private versus state/local ownership.
- Full-time versus part-time work.
- Union versus nonunion status.
- Time-based versus incentive-based pay.
- Establishment size.
- Wage categories or bands.
- Census regions/divisions and selected major metropolitan areas.
- Work levels, particularly in MWE.

Industry and occupation coding uses **NAICS** and **SOC**, with earlier publications using predecessor systems.

### Geographic limits

Direct NCS products are **not designed to produce a complete set of estimates for individual states**. BLS can consider special tabulations, but sample support and confidentiality constrain detail.

**MWE is different:** its combination with OEWS supports national, state, metropolitan, and nonmetropolitan estimates. BLS says MWE excludes Guam, Puerto Rico, and the Virgin Islands because those territories are outside NCS scope.

Sources: [ECI questions and answers](https://www.bls.gov/eci/questions-and-answers.htm), [special-tabulation guidance](https://www.bls.gov/ecec/overview/ncs-data-requests.htm), [MWE geographic scope](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/mwe/concepts.htm).

## 5. Collection and statistical methodology

### Sampling

Current ECI methods describe a **two-stage probability sample**:

1. Select establishments, using probability proportional to employment size.
2. Select occupations/jobs within sampled establishments.

Larger establishments have greater selection probabilities, but their records are not simply treated as one equally weighted observation.

The establishment frame draws on **Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW)** information. BLS documentation describes 24 sampling areas: 15 large areas and the remaining portions of nine census divisions.

### Collection

Trained BLS field economists collect information through interviews and employer records, including job descriptions and benefit documents. Contacts can involve telephone, email, mail, or personal visits.

The methods chapter emphasizes conversational interviewing rather than a conventional standalone questionnaire. The OMB package also lists collection/update forms and electronic update mechanisms; archivists should preserve both the methods narrative and the approved instruments.

For ECI and ECEC, reference periods are the pay periods including the **12th of March, June, September, and December**. Benefits incidence and key provisions generally have a **March reference date**; detailed provisions can represent an entire year.

### Rotation

Current design documentation describes:

- Three private-industry rotation groups.
- A state/local government group.
- A separate aircraft-manufacturing group.

Private-industry and aircraft samples rotate approximately every three years, with scheduling exceptions; state/local samples rotate approximately every ten years.

This is an overlapping establishment/job panel—not a longitudinal survey following the same individual employees.

### Estimation

**ECI:** a modified Laspeyres index, using matched job observations and fixed industry/occupation employment weights. “Pure cost change” is BLS’s description of its composition-control objective; it does not mean the index eliminates every possible within-category change.

**ECEC:** weighted compensation-cost levels, benchmarked using QCEW and Current Employment Statistics information. Benefit-cost averages generally include workers with **zero employer cost** for that benefit, not just participating workers.

**Benefits:** weighted estimates of access, participation, provisions, and related measures, with nonresponse adjustments and benchmarking.

**MWE:** modeled allocation of OEWS occupational employment using relationships between wages and job characteristics observed in NCS. Broader-area relationships are assumed to apply to smaller areas. Accordingly, a local MWE estimate is not simply the mean of a large directly observed NCS sample in that locality.

Sources: [sampling and rotation](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/eci/design.htm), [collection](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/eci/data.htm), [ECI calculation](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/eci/calculation.htm), [ECEC calculation](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ecec/calculation.htm), [MWE assumptions](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/mwe/calculation.htm).

## 6. History and lineage

NCS consolidates a much older federal compensation-statistics tradition.

| Date | Milestone |
|---|---|
| **1885** | First BLS occupational-wage study |
| **1938–1939** | Industry wage surveys supporting the Fair Labor Standards Act |
| **1948 onward** | Community wage surveys; later Area Wage Surveys |
| **1959** | Employer Expenditures for Employee Compensation introduced |
| **1960** | National professional, administrative, technical, and clerical pay survey introduced |
| **1975** | ECI introduced; private-industry wage results first published in June 1976 |
| **1979** | Employee Benefits Survey introduced |
| **1981** | ECI expanded to total compensation, benefits, and state/local government |
| **1986** | ECEC introduced |
| **1991** | Occupational Compensation Survey combined several earlier wage surveys |
| **1996** | COMP2000 consolidated occupational compensation, ECI/ECEC, and benefits collection |
| **2000** | COMP2000 renamed National Compensation Survey |
| **2002** | Quarterly ECEC releases began |
| **2004–2006** | Major transitions to NAICS/SOC classifications; ECI rebased to December 2005 = 100 |
| **2008–2009** | Selected metropolitan ECI/ECEC outputs and expanded benefits reporting |
| **2016** | ECEC benchmarking expanded to include establishment size |
| **2021** | New OEWS model-based estimation method introduced into 2021 MWE |
| **2025–2026** | Methods documentation reorganized; collection changes and future ECI changes announced |

**Cataloging implication:** “NCS began in 1996,” “the name NCS dates to 2000,” and “ECI began in 1975” describe different aspects of the lineage. None is a universal start date for all NCS-related files.

Earlier benefits surveys also differed in coverage—for example, establishment-size coverage and whether private or state/local workers were included. Historical data must not be treated as automatically comparable to current all-size civilian estimates.

Sources: [BLS compensation-survey history](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ncs/history.htm), [MWE methodology FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/mwe/faq.htm).

BLS’s data directory states that benefits databases cover **1985–2006** and **2010 onward**, while **2007–2009 data must be obtained from benefits publications**.

- Ownership.
- Industry and occupation.
- Worker and establishment characteristics.
- Geography.
- Reference period.

**NCS employer/job microdata are not an ordinary public-use download.** Researchers should consult [BLS Restricted Data Access](https://www.bls.gov/rda/home.htm), confirm the available NCS files and years, and submit an appropriate research proposal. ### Confidentiality

BLS uses responses for statistical purposes and screens published figures to prevent identification of respondents. CIPSEA provides an important legal foundation for protecting information collected under a statistical confidentiality pledge.

A nuance in historical documentation: the 2018 supporting statement says the standard pledge was not automatically extended to state/local entities unless requested, because their information could be public record. Do not assume identical pledge language across respondent types and years.

### Reuse rights

BLS states its published material is **public domain**, except previously copyrighted photographs and illustrations. Permission is not required to reuse public-domain statistics, although BLS requests source attribution. The BLS emblem is a protected trademark.

Sources: [special-tabulation policy](https://www.bls.gov/ecec/overview/ncs-data-requests.htm), [collection/confidentiality documentation](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ncs/data.htm), [historical pledge detail](https://omb.report/icr/201712-1220-003/doc/81468201.pdf), [copyright policy](https://www.bls.gov/opub/copyright-information.htm).

## 9. Data quality, comparability, and misuse risks

### Core limitations

1. **Sampling error:** estimates come from a sample, not a census. Use published standard errors or relative standard errors where available.
2. **Nonsampling error:** nonresponse, reporting errors, coding, missing data, and imputation can affect estimates.
3. **Sparse detail:** detailed geographic/occupational/benefit cells may be unavailable or suppressed.
4. **Means are not medians:** average compensation is not necessarily a typical worker’s compensation.
5. **Employer costs are not take-home pay:** they include costs workers do not receive as cash.
6. **Hourly cost uses hours worked:** paid leave and other annual costs can make this different from cost per paid hour.
7. **ECEC changes are not ECI changes:** ECEC reflects current workforce composition; ECI aims to control industry/occupation composition.
8. **Access is not use or adequacy:** having a medical plan available does not establish affordability, adequate coverage, or actual service use.
9. **Group gaps are not causal effects:** union/nonunion or public/private differences can reflect occupation, industry, work status, and other composition.
10. **MWE carries model assumptions:** detailed local figures borrow information from broader areas.
11. **Limited demographic analysis:** standard public outputs are job/employer-oriented, not a comprehensive race, sex, age, or household-income microdataset.
12. **Historical definitions change:** classifications, sample coverage, benefit questions, and publication criteria must be checked by vintage.

### Revisions

ECI seasonal adjustment uses **X-13ARIMA-SEATS**. BLS recalculates factors and revises the most recent **five years** of seasonally adjusted data annually.

A current API extraction can consequently differ from what users saw at the original release. Preserve **first-release and revised vintages**, especially for real-time forecasting or analysis of policy decisions.

Sources: [ECI calculation and revisions](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/eci/calculation.htm), [ECEC interpretation](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ecec/calculation.htm), [MWE publication criteria and uncertainty](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/mwe/calculation.htm).

## 10. Recent developments requiring preservation attention

### Proposed removal of collection elements

A July 2025 Federal Register notice proposed removing resource-intensive elements BLS described as lightly used, including:

- Sick-leave carryover details.
- Retiree life insurance.
- Third-party health-plan administration and stop-loss protection.
- Employee nonmedical premiums.
- Certain employer nonmedical premiums.
- Details of frozen defined-benefit plans.
- “Other benefits” plans or provisions.

The notice also proposed discontinuing **workers’ compensation insurance collection**, citing low response rates and concern that further collection efforts could damage response for other benefits.

These were **proposals in that notice**. The 2026 revised collection was subsequently approved, but the implementation date of every listed element should be verified against the final supporting statement and product-specific notices.

Source: [July 2025 Federal Register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/07/16/2025-13287/information-collection-activities-comment-request).

### Announced ECI change

BLS explicitly announces that the **January 2027 release of December 2026 data** will:

- Replace the 2021 fixed employment weights with **2025 OEWS weights**.
- Remove **workers’ compensation costs** from ECI calculations.

This is an announced future change as of the research date—not a change to assume has already occurred.

**Preservation consequence:** capture the notice, the last pre-change release, the first post-change release, and BLS’s transition explanations. Distinguish reweighting from a change in the components being measured.

Source: [BLS ECI transition notice](https://www.bls.gov/eci/notices/2026/eci-2025-fixed-weights-and-removing-workers-compensation.htm).

### Funding interruptions and response

BLS reports that the October–November 2025 lapse in appropriations delayed the September 2025 ECI release by more than five weeks and reduced response:

- Survey response rate: **45.1% in June to 40.6% in September**.
- Usable rate at update: **83.1% to 74.4%**.

These are different rate definitions, not interchangeable measures. They document both dissemination delay and collection disruption.

Source: [ECI questions and answers](https://www.bls.gov/eci/questions-and-answers.htm).

## 11. Recommended preservation and cataloging plan

*The following are recommendations, not claims about BLS’s internal records-retention policy.*

### Preserve a collection, not one file

Create a parent record for **NCS**, with child collections for:

- ECI.
- ECEC.
- Employee Benefits.
- MWE.
- Historical wage products and predecessor surveys.
- Methods, legal/administrative records, and transition notices.

For MWE, explicitly record **both NCS and OEWS** as inputs.

### Minimum archival package

Preserve:

1. Numerical files in their original formats.
2. Series dictionaries, code lists, and file-layout documentation.
3. News releases and technical notes.
4. Standard-error/RSE tables and response-rate documentation.
5. Methods chapters, including archived versions.
6. Benefit glossaries and collection instruments.
7. NAICS, SOC, and geographic-definition versions.
8. Seasonal factors, reweighting notices, and revision notices.
9. OMB supporting statements, approvals, and Federal Register notices.
10. Special tabulations and their explanatory correspondence, where releasable.

### Essential metadata

Record at least:

- Product and series ID.
- Full measure title and unit.
- Population/ownership and geography.
- Industry and occupation codes **and versions**.
- Worker/establishment characteristics.
- Benefit component and denominator.
- Reference period and publication date.
- Retrieval date and release vintage.
- Seasonal-adjustment and nominal/real-dollar status.
- Index reference base, where relevant.
- Suppression/missing-value symbols and footnotes.
- Methodology version and discontinuity flags.
- Original URL, checksum, and transformation history.

### Practical safeguards

- Retain originals; create normalized CSV or Parquet derivatives separately.
- Keep suppression, unavailable, and zero values distinct.
- Preserve HTML and spreadsheets alongside PDFs.
- Test archive coverage of 2007–2009 benefits publications.
- Avoid relying solely on mutable “latest release” URLs.
- Snapshot data before scheduled revisions and transitions.
- Do not place restricted respondent records in a public repository.
- Preserve documented variable removals: disappearance from a file must not be mistaken for disappearance of a benefit.

**Unverified archival questions:** this research did not establish an NCS-specific NARA disposition schedule, a guaranteed permanent public archive of every microdata vintage, or a complete inventory of all surviving historical files. Those require direct inquiry to BLS and, where appropriate, federal records officials.

## 12. Recommendations for policy activists and data scientists

### For policy work

NCS is particularly useful for examining:

- Paid-leave disparities.
- Health-plan access and premium burdens.
- Retirement-plan availability.
- Differences between full- and part-time jobs.
- Compensation by employer size and union status.
- Whether nominal compensation growth exceeds inflation.

For advocacy concerning collection changes, explain the **specific public use** of a threatened variable. BLS’s stated reliance on database use and customer inquiries means that demonstrated demand can matter. PRA comment periods provide a formal channel, though the notices discussed above are historical rather than necessarily open now.

Avoid using NCS alone to establish individual discrimination, causal policy impacts, or precise small-area conditions.

### For reproducible analysis

- Choose the product before downloading: **ECI for change, ECEC for cost levels, Benefits for coverage/provisions, MWE for detailed modeled occupational wages**.
- Pin the data vintage.
- Validate series IDs and units against dictionaries.
- Carry uncertainty and footnotes into analytical outputs.
- Flag classifications and component changes.
- Do not splice discontinued and current series without a documented bridge.
- Supplement NCS with appropriate sources—for example, CPS/ACS for worker demographics and household circumstances, or OEWS/QCEW for different occupational and geographic needs.

---

## Overall assessment

The National Compensation Survey is **national statistical infrastructure**, not merely a wage table. Its distinctive value is the combination of compensation-cost trends, employer cost levels, benefits availability and provisions, and detailed job information.

For preservationists, the highest priorities are **historical publications, metadata, release vintages, and transition documentation**. For analysts, the principal challenge is choosing the correct measure and respecting population, denominator, and modeling limits. For policy advocates, its strongest contribution is public evidence about job quality and compensation—but the scope of that evidence depends on continued collection, adequate response, and preservation of variables that may otherwise disappear.

# National Compensation Survey: dataset risk assessment

**Assessment date: October 9, 2026**

**Overall finding:** The strongest documented risks are **loss of detail, interruptions to timely publication, and diminished institutional capacity**—not wholesale disappearance of historical NCS data. Historical releases remain accessible, and collection approval extends through May 2029. However, BLS has approved collection reductions, announced changes to compensation measures, and experienced both publication delays and removal of its commissioner.

## Scope and scoring approach

This assessment covers the **NCS program and its public products: ECI, ECEC, Employee Benefits, and its contribution to Modeled Wage Estimates**. Confidential respondent microdata were never generally downloadable, so their restricted status is not treated as a removal.

I distinguish:

- **Deletion of historical observations** from discontinuation of future collection.
- **Enacted funding** from presidential budget requests.
- **Agency-wide risks** from demonstrated NCS-specific changes.
- **Documented methodological revisions** from unsupported allegations of manipulation.

The ratings apply your rubric’s triggers; they are not numerical probabilities of eventual deletion. Where several levels have supporting evidence, I select the highest **substantiated applicable** level.

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

- **No Known Issue — supported.** BLS maintains an [ECI archive spanning releases from 1976 onward](https://www.bls.gov/bls/news-release/eci.htm). I also successfully retrieved the [September 2024 release and its numerical tables](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/eci_10312024.htm). BLS continues to identify historical benefits estimates as available through spreadsheets and database tools.
- **Moderate Risk — not established for historical removal.** Planned removal of workers’ compensation and other collection elements affects future measurements; the notices do not establish that those elements have been erased from historical releases. BLS explicitly says that previously published paid-family-leave estimates through 2023 **will continue to be available**, despite a revised definition. See [Employee Benefits questions and answers](https://www.bls.gov/ebs/questions-and-answers.htm).
- **High Risk / Gone — no supporting evidence found.** I found no documented withdrawal of historical NCS files or disappearance of all pre-current-cycle data.

**Qualification:** ECI seasonally adjusted values undergo documented routine revisions. Historical accessibility therefore does not mean every current database value is identical to its first-release value. Such revisions are not, by themselves, evidence of destructive alteration. See [ECI calculation methods](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/eci/calculation.htm).

  The second activity includes NCS but also other programs; it is not an NCS-only staffing count. FTE figures should not be equated directly with a count of individual employees separated.
- **No Known Issue — supported by enacted funding alone.**
  - Total BLS funding: **$703.952 million in FY2025 to $708.500 million in FY2026**, a nominal increase of approximately **0.6%**.
  - Compensation and Working Conditions: **$92.354 million to $91.500 million**, approximately **0.9% lower**.
  - These enacted changes do **not** meet a 10% or 20% budget-cut threshold.
- **Proposed funding pressure:** FY2027 requests **$667.952 million** for BLS, approximately **5.7% below FY2026**, and **$86.822 million** for Compensation and Working Conditions, approximately **5.1% lower**. These are **requests, not proof of enacted FY2027 cuts**.
- **Gone — no evidence.** Neither staffing nor funding has been wholly terminated.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

Actual commissioner removal meets the rubric’s High Risk criterion. Staffing figures independently support Moderate Risk; enacted budgets do not support a large-cut claim.

### Evidence by risk level

- **Moderate Risk — directly supported.**
  - NCS collection changes were proposed after January 2025, subsequently approved, and include forthcoming changes to compensation measures.
  - The FY2027 budget continues a proposal to reorganize **BLS, Census, and BEA at the Department of Commerce**. BLS describes savings from attrition and reorganization and proposes making recent staffing reductions permanent.
  - A departmental transfer could require changes to stewardship or dissemination arrangements, but no NCS website migration or archive-deletion plan was established.

  Sources: [Federal Register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/07/16/2025-13287/information-collection-activities-comment-request), [OMB approval](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202506-1220-001), [FY2027 budget justification](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/general/budget/2027/CBJ-2027-V3-01.pdf).

  - Presidential accusations and commissioner removal demonstrate political pressure on BLS. Administration advisers publicly defended the removal. See [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/white-house-defends-firing-labor-official-critics-warn-trust-erosion-2025-08-04/).
  - However, those allegations concerned employment estimates, not demonstrated manipulation of NCS.
  - I found no substantiated NCS-specific Presidential Action-driven ICR or ideological notice directing suppression.
  - Crucially, the workers’ compensation removal rationale was published **in 2023**, before the current administration.
- **No Known Issue — not appropriate.** Notable collection changes and reorganization proposals exist.
- **Gone — no evidence.** NCS continues.

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

Changes and pending institutional proposals are documented, but the evidence does not establish the rubric’s stronger NCS-specific administration-directed suppression trigger. Commissioner removal is scored separately under Staffing and Funding.
